W7224857431.abstract: Machine learning (ML) techniques are increasingly explored to analyse gravitational wave (GW) data expected from the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). At the same time, advances in quantum computing have stimulated interest in quantum machine learning as a potential alternative to conventional approaches. We investigate the applicability of quantum, hybrid quantum-classical, and classical ML models to two tasks relevant for LISA observations of massive black hole binaries: GW signal detection and merger prediction. Using the Sangria dataset from the LISA Data Challenge, we benchmark several quantum architectures, including variational quantum classifiers (VQCs), post VQC hybrid models, quantum kernel methods, data reuploading classifiers, and quantum long short-term memory (QLSTM) networks, against classical support vector machines, multilayer perceptrons, recurrent neural networks, and LSTM networks. The models are trained on labelled data derived from the Sangria training dataset and evaluated on the corresponding blind dataset. For signal detection, several quantum models match or outperform classical baselines. In particular, the best performing hybrid post VQC architecture correctly identifies all signal samples in the blind dataset, while the standard VQC and data reuploading classifier achieve competitive detection rates. For merger detection and coalescence time estimation, however, the standard VQC emerges as the most reliable model, successfully localising all detected merger events with the lowest localisation errors. We further analyse the trade-offs between predictive performance, model complexity, and quantum circuit resources. Our results indicate that, although no universal quantum advantage is observed, selected quantum models can provide practical benefits for specific GW analysis tasks and represent promising candidates for future LISA data analysis pipelines.

W7224907701.abstract: Clinical text summarization has emerged as an important application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) to efficiently summarize the rapidly growing volume of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) and other medical documents. This survey reviews recent advancements in clinical text summarization by analyzing twenty representative studies that employ transformer-based models, Large Language Models (LLMs), hybrid approaches, semantic graph techniques, multimodal learning, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). The survey compares widely used models, including Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformers (BART), Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer(T5), Pre-training with Extracted Gap-sentences for Abstractive Summarization(PEGASUS), Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers for Biomedical Text Mining (BioBERT), Clinical Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers(ClinicalBERT), Generative Pre-trained Transformer(GPT), and Large Language Model Meta AI (LLaMA), based on their methodologies, performance, strengths, limitations, and evaluation metrics. The analysis indicates that transformer-based and hybrid models produce more coherent, context-aware, and clinically relevant summaries than traditional extractive methods; however, challenges such as factual hallucination, limited explainability, privacy concerns, computational complexity, and the lack of standardized evaluation datasets continue to hinder their practical adoption. Based on these findings, the survey identifies key research gaps and highlights future research directions toward developing accurate, explainable, multimodal, and clinically reliable clinical text summarization systems to support efficient healthcare decision-making and improve patient care.

W7225062460.abstract: Integrated circuits (ICs) have played a fundamental role in the development of modern electronics, computing, and information technologies. This review presents an overview of the historical evolution of IC technology, from the invention of the transistor and the first integrated circuits to the emergence of very-large-scale integration, advanced complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) technologies, and nanoscale semiconductor devices. Particular attention is given to the physical principles of semiconductor integration, transistor scaling, lithographic techniques, and advances in semiconductor materials. Major technological milestones, including the development of microprocessors, system-on-chip architectures, three-dimensional integration, and chiplet-based designs, are discussed. Applications in computing, telecommunications, artificial intelligence, automotive electronics, and industrial systems are highlighted. Furthermore, challenges associated with power consumption, thermal management, fabrication complexity, and physical scaling limitations are examined. Emerging technologies and future research directions are discussed to provide a comprehensive perspective on the continued evolution of integrated circuits.

W7225095053.abstract: Academic program analysis plays a critical role in supporting curriculum design, academic advising, and student decision-making. However, most curriculum frameworks are provided in semi-structured textual formats, where relationships among knowledge blocks, courses, learning outcomes, and prerequisite structures remain implicit and difficult to analyze systematically. This limitation hinders the ability of stakeholders to gain insights into curriculum structure, such as knowledge coverage, learning pathways, and graduation requirements. This paper proposes a knowledge graph reasoning framework for syllabi analysis, integrating Large Language Model (LLM)-based structured extraction with graph-based modeling and reasoning techniques. A curriculum knowledge model is first defined to represent academic programs. A semi-automated data pipeline is then developed to extract structured information from curriculum documents and construct a knowledge graph in Neo4j. On top of this graph, a reasoning engine is designed to support query-based and rule-based analysis, enabling stakeholders to explore curriculum structures and answer practical questions. The framework is validated using real-world curriculum data from a university program. The findings highlight the potential of combining LLM-based extraction with knowledge graph reasoning for scalable and insightful curriculum analytics.

W7225148783.abstract: Knowledge is how understanding accumulates across people and generations: durable records that outlive their producers and that others can check, combine, teach, and correct. AI agents are now built and run by many independent users and organizations, and each agent is upgraded, replaced, or retired within months. Yet what an agent learns stays trapped in model parameters, a transient context window, or a system-specific memory store that is appended to and retrieved from rather than processed. We argue that the next generation of AI should be knowledge-centric, built around an explicit, continuously evolving knowledge layer independent of any single agent. In this loop, agents discover knowledge from their environments and trajectories; the layer internalizes it by turning fragmented, heterogeneous records and experience into composable, revisable understanding; and agents across systems and generations use the result and return new outcomes for revision. While discovery and use have advanced rapidly with large language model agents, internalization remains the bottleneck. We argue that internalization should become a persistent object of training and maintenance-centered on condition-preserving conceptualization of events and deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning across noisy, heterogeneous representations (text, tables, graphs, rules, and programs). To power this layer, we call for knowledge foundation models that provide shared neural capacity for knowledge computation, and outline a research agenda showing how an explicit knowledge layer delivers reuse, cost efficiency, auditability, and continuity across agent generations.

W7225225918.abstract: Background: Natural products remain an important source of therapeutic agents, but their discovery is constrained by chemical complexity, time-consuming isolation, difficult structure elucidation, and high attrition rates. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning, graph neural networks, and generative AI, offers computational approaches to address these challenges. Method: This narrative review examines peer-reviewed, English-language literature published between 2021 and 2026, retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The selected literature was analyzed using thematic qualitative synthesis to identify AI applications, reported contributions, and persistent limitations across the natural product discovery pipeline. Problem Identification: Despite growing interest in AI-assisted drug discovery, the extent to which current methods address the limitations of conventional approaches remains uncertain. Key concerns include data quality, model reliability, interpretability, and the need for experimental validation. Results: AI applications cover target identification, biosynthetic gene cluster mining, virtual screening, structure elucidation, network pharmacology, generative molecular design, and absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) prediction. These methods can help prioritize candidate compounds and predict potential biological activities. However, data scarcity and bias, inconsistent evaluation practices, limited interpretability, and insufficient experimental validation remain significant barriers. Explainable AI, multi-omics integration, and self-driving laboratories represent promising developments, although their practical contributions require further validation. Conclusion: AI can support and accelerate selected stages of natural product-based drug discovery but cannot replace experimental testing or the expertise of natural product chemists and pharmacologists.

W7225271207.abstract: Solid electrolytes are widely expected to replace flammable liquid electrolytes in lithium batteries, yet cell-level progress has lagged behind the large gains in bulk ionic conductivity achieved over the past decade. This review argues that the electrode–electrolyte interface, rather than the bulk electrolyte, should be the unit of design, and examines the consequences of this view for engineering practice and for artificial intelligence (AI)-guided discovery. Using a documented, non-systematic literature selection (mainly 2018–2026, with earlier foundational work), we first re-examine the safety premise: removing the liquid removes one fuel, but thermal-runaway pathways remain through cathode oxygen release, lithium-metal reactivity, and stored electrical energy. We then compare oxide, sulfide, halide/oxyhalide, solid polymer, gel/quasi-solid, and composite electrolytes, together with the cathodes and anodes they must contact, explain how solid–solid interfaces form and degrade chemically, electrochemically, and mechanically, and critically assess the experimental techniques used to diagnose them. An area-specific resistance analysis indicates that once separators are about 30 µm thick and conductivities exceed ∼1 mS cm⁻¹, interfacial and composite-electrode resistances, rather than bulk conductivity, usually dominate ohmic loss. Three ‘translation gaps’ are identified in which bulk metrics or computational descriptors (ionic conductivity, thermodynamic stability windows and elastic-modulus criteria) fail to predict cell behaviour. AI studies are graded on two complementary scales: the type of validation (Levels L1–L4) and the cell-level validation scale (grades A–D). Experimentally validated successes are concentrated in bulk properties and low-dimensional synthesis optimisation, whereas interface prediction remains largely computational, trained on small datasets and bounded by an experimental ‘noise floor’ (inter-laboratory relative standard deviations of 35–50% in the conductivity of identical samples). We propose an Interface Co-Design Framework with four operationally defined validity gates, chemical pairing, mechanical contact, transport translation, and manufacturing and safety validation, together with measurable reporting criteria and a Minimum Interface Data Record. AI is likely to accelerate practical solid-state batteries only if its training labels describe the failure modes that limit cells and if electrolyte, electrode, interface and processing are optimised jointly rather than sequentially.

W7225297620.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly reshaping software engineering (SE) across the development lifecycle. This review synthesises 113 peer-reviewed journal studies and organises the literature around five research questions and four application areas: code generation, testing and debugging, human–AI collaboration, and quality assurance. The reviewed studies show substantial progress in natural-language-to-code generation, context-aware programming, automated testing, fault localisation, program repair, and AI-assisted development. At the same time, persistent challenges remain in semantic correctness, non-deterministic outputs, software security, maintainability, verification, and evaluation consistency. Drawing these findings together, the paper presents a lifecycle mapping, a closed-loop AI-driven software engineering framework, and a four-dimension taxonomy to organise existing research and clarify connections across previously fragmented areas. Overall, generative AI is moving software engineering from a largely deterministic and human-centred workflow toward a more probabilistic and AI-enhanced engineering process. Further progress will depend on stronger verification, security, reliability, maintainability, and appropriately calibrated human oversight.

W7225330753.abstract: Materials discovery increasingly depends on a multiscale ecosystem of simulations, experiments, and shared facilities, yet advances in individual AI tools do not by themselves connect the decisions that link these components. This gap is especially severe in all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), whose development couples electrochemical performance to interfacial stability, mechanics, processing, manufacturability, reliability, safety, and cost. Here we argue that AI agents could support ASSB development toward commercial viability by maintaining a shared decision–evidence state that links materials discovery and optimization to cell-level validation and manufacturing constraints. We develop this argument through three complementary dimensions of scientific agency: coordination across heterogeneous resources, method augmentation across models and scales, and project-level adaptation over time. Cross-domain demonstrations establish several relevant capability primitives, including stateful tool planning, task execution, and delegated analysis. Agents should therefore be evaluated as supporting infrastructure for concurrent ASSB engineering rather than as autonomous replacements for scientific expertise. Their value ultimately lies in driving materials development in the context of interfaces, cell architectures, and manufacturing processes toward the performance, reliability, safety, and cost requirements of ASSB commercialization. context & scale Commercializing all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) requires more than identifying high-performing materials: ion transport, interphase chemistry, mechanics, processing, cell architecture, reliability, safety, and cost impose coupled constraints that can invalidate otherwise promising candidates. This Perspective argues that AI agents could serve as auditable infrastructure, maintaining a decision-evidence state that connects objectives, specimen histories, models, uncertainties, actions, and validation to support ASSB development. Such infrastructure could broaden research across instruments and engineering stages, strengthen validation by linking atomistic, mesoscale, continuum, and experimental descriptions, and preserve evidence and revisions throughout development cycles. Future efforts should move beyond task-level demonstrations toward systematic ASSB development, establishing whether agents can contribute to the development of reliable and economically viable ASSB systems.

W7225342750.abstract: Introduction Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the greatest global public health threats, contributing to an estimated 4.95 million deaths annually worldwide (Murray et al., 2022). AMR is driven by inappropriate antimicrobial use in human medicine, veterinary practice, agriculture, and environmental contamination. The One Health approach, integrating human, animal, and environmental health, provides a comprehensive framework for addressing AMR. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers promising opportunities to strengthen AMR surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship (WHO, 2023). To systematically review applications of AI technologies in AMR surveillance, prediction, diagnosis, prevention, management, and antimicrobial discovery across human, animal, and environmental health sectors. Methods A systematic review was conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and IEEE Xplore were searched for studies published from January 2015 to March 2026. Search terms included “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “predictive analytics,” “antimicrobial resistance,” “antibiotic resistance,” and “One Health.” Eligible studies evaluated AI applications for AMR surveillance, diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, resistance prediction, or antimicrobial discovery in human, veterinary, agricultural, or environmental settings. Results The search identified 2,146 records, of which 58 studies met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 20 (34.5%) focused on AMR surveillance, 16 (27.6%) on predictive modelling, 13 (22.4%) on rapid diagnostics, and 9 (15.5%) on antimicrobial discovery. AI-assisted diagnostic platforms reduced the time required for pathogen identification and susceptibility testing compared with conventional laboratory methods. Conclusion AI demonstrates substantial potential to transform the global response to AMR. Across One Health sectors, AI can strengthen surveillance, improve antimicrobial stewardship, accelerate diagnostics, predict resistance patterns, and support discovery of novel antimicrobial agents.
